title: The odds average the bettors
hook: One bettor says 80%, another 40%. The odds don't say 60%. Whose opinion counts more?

doesNotKnow: that when bettors split their money in proportion to their beliefs, the market's implied chance is the wealth-weighted average belief

misconception: The odds reflect the simple average opinion, or the loudest bettor's.
objective: The learner can explain that $300 x 80% + $100 x 40% = $280 of a $400 pool on A gives implied odds of 70%, because each belief counts in proportion to the money behind it, not the simple average of 60%.

claims.text: With bettor 1 putting $300 x 80% = $240 and bettor 2 $100 x 40% = $40 on A, $280 of the $400 pool is on A, so the implied chance is 70%, not the simple average of 60%.
With equal money the implied chance equals the simple average of beliefs; when bettor 2 holds more, it moves toward bettor 2's 40% (with $100 and $300 it is 50%).
claims.source: Equal wealth w: (w p1 + w p2) / 2w = (p1 + p2) / 2. Preset 'Bettor 2 richer': (100 x 0.8 + 300 x 0.4) / 400 = 0.50. Demo.tsx pool().

claims.text: When every bettor splits all their money by belief, the implied chance is the wealth-weighted average belief: each opinion counts in proportion to the money behind it.
claims.source: Money on A = sum of w_i p_i; pool = sum of w_i; ratio = sum (w_i / W) p_i. Demo.tsx pool().

claims.text: Splitting all your money by belief is how a bettor who maximises the logarithm of their wealth bets in a pari-mutuel market.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg 2010, ch. 22; Kelly 1956 (Bell System Technical Journal 35). Fact-checker to confirm.

claims.text: The lesson is a simplified model: two bettors, no house cut, everyone bets all their money by belief.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: no house cut; all money bet by belief' and the reveal's last line.

recall.question: Ana ($100) thinks a team wins 90%; Ben ($300) thinks 50%. Each bets all their money in proportion to belief. What chance do the odds imply?
recall.why: $90 + $150 = $240 of the $400 pool is on the team: 60%. Ben's belief counts three times as much because he has three times the money.
